speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that getting away to the Moon is not always possible, and that the terrible realities of every day life bring us back to much gloomier thoughts.
Hon. members undoubtedly recall the great disasters of May 1950 at Rimouski and Cabano. This morning, it is at Notre-Dame-du-Lac, a locality near Cabano, that a tragic fire took the lives of more than 50 aged people and caused injuries to more than 20 others at the rest home "Le Repos du Vieillard", thus bringing consternation to that locality which celebrates this year the centennial of its foundation.
To the stricken families and to all the population as well, I wish to extend the expression of my heartfelt condolences, and I am sure that all hon. members will wish to join in this expression of sympathy.
I ask the government to take all necessary steps to bring those people immediate assistance.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure of drawing Your Honour's attention and the attention of all hon. members to the presence in your gallery of several distinguished visitors. speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WELCOME AND TRIBUTE TO APOLLO 11 ASTRONAUTS BY HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: The venture of these three brave men into the unknown stirred the imagination and the pride of all Canadians. This country is not so old nor so well explored, that either the experience of the frontier or the taste of adventure is forgotten. We are close in time and in space to wilderness. In our blood-or perhaps just in our secret desires-is found the spirit of such as Hudson and Cartier, Palliser and Steffanson. The exploits of our visitors today proved that the age of exploration is not over and we are glad. They proved too that there is new meaning in the heavens, and we are better for it. Mr. Speaker, we are delighted to have with us these courageous men and their equally brave wives.

subtopic: WELCOME AND TRIBUTE TO APOLLO 11 ASTRONAUTS BY HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased on behalf of my colleagues and myself to be associated with the welcome the Prime Minister has extended to Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin, and their wives. subtopic: WELCOME AND TRIBUTE TO APOLLO 11 ASTRONAUTS BY HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WELCOME AND TRIBUTE TO APOLLO 11 ASTRONAUTS BY HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Whatever our admiration of their courage and our awe at their accomplishments, I think the dominant feeling of all of us besides that of pleasure is one of humility.

Distinguished visitors have, of course, come to this Chamber before, but there have been none before who have symbolized the breaking of old concepts in the way these men do. We must remember that, while they were alone in space, the responsibility for making this space age serve man is one we must all meet together.
I do not wish to be too solemn, but as a practical man who watched these men in space there were some considerations of a practical nature which occurred to me. However, I believe these would be better presented to these gentlemen in private.
It will, of course, be many years before the full significance of this exploit is realized. In 1492 it was difficult for contemporaries to visualize all the consequences of the discovery by Columbus. It is a sobering thought that we today are one of those consequences and that an equally significant development may follow from the exploration of these men.
To be serious, Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to join with the Prime Minister and all members of the House in welcoming these three brave men and their wives.

subtopic: WELCOME AND TRIBUTE TO APOLLO 11 ASTRONAUTS BY HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: WELCOME AND TRIBUTE TO APOLLO 11 ASTRONAUTS BY HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all Canadians will echo the sentiments expressed by the Prime Minister in paying tribute to our distinguished guests. They honour us by their presence here today and we honour them for the great contribution they have made to man's enlarging knowledge of the universe in which we live.
We pay tribute also to their courage, skill and the teamwork which made the venture of Apollo 11 such an outstanding success. We also pay tribute to the thousands of men who made their trip possible and to their great country, the United States, which has been in the forefront of the exploration of space.
The names of Neil Armstrong, Mike Collins and Edwin Aldrin will go down in history among the great pathfinders of space.
I am convinced that this is only the beginning of man's exploration of our solar system. The day undoubtedly will come when other earthmen will reach out to other planets and even break through into our sidereal system.
The astronauts whom we honour here today represent a challenge to the governments and legislators of the world to match their achievement in landing on the moon with similar advances here on earth.

Two of the astronauts landed near the Sea of Tranquillity. I think we can assure them that we in this Parliament will do our part in trying to make this earth a place of tranquillity and security for all mankind.

Mr. Speaker, when this bill was last before the House I outlined some of the reasons the people of the Atlantic provinces have lost all faith and hope that the government will give them the opportunity to receive equal treatment with other Canadians. I tried to place on the record some of the ways in which this government has endeavoured to ignore the justifiable arguments presented by the business communities why a transportation policy should have been introduced in this region a long time ago.
As a result of the government's failure, the people in the Atlantic provinces are faced with almost impossible burdens industrially and are unable to attract new industry. In 1967 the government allowed the railways to impose new l.c.l. charges on the shippers in the region. After about a year and a half the government gave the trucking industry certain incentives the railways already had, making it possible for them to compete with the railways. This resulted in the shippers in the Atlantic region being placed on a somewhat better footing.
Since then, the government has allowed the railways to increase their rates on carload lot shipments. The rates freeze has been lifted before the promised transportation policy for the region has been introduced. Although the government has talked so much about elimination of regional economic disparity, there is no way in which it can justify its actions in the field of transportation.

At the present time the florist industry in the area is being placed under new burdensome express charges as a result of the action of the railways. Every time we turn around something new is happening; either more layoffs under the guise of increased efficiency or closures of one type of operation or another. Only recently my colleague the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacEwan) appeared before an inquiry relating to the elimination of air services in the Pictou County area. Every step this government agrees to is a backwards step, and every step it takes represents damage to the economy of the Atlantic region.
We watch the spiralling unemployment rates in the area every winter. This is the same story every winter. Sometimes during the summer we look at our unemployment rate and feel that maybe things are getting better, but when the fall comes it is the same old story of an unemployment rate that is two or three times the national average. We then read in the newspapers about this or that industry having to close down because it is impossible to compete with industry in the rest of Canada.
One of the basic reasons for this problem is the fact that we have been the captive of the railways. Our industries have not been able to compete with similar industries in the central part of Canada. Surely, by now this government should have conceived a policy that would place industry in the Atlantic part of Canada on an equal footing with industry in the remainder of the nation. Industry in our area of Canada could then produce the same product and move it anywhere in this nation in competition with industry in Ontario rather than being forced to pay more for the movement of these goods than if that industry were located in central Canada. Surely, this is the only way that we can exist as a viable entity in Canada.
This certainly is not the case today. It will not be the case tomorrow, and it may well never be the case if this government does not soon move in this direction. One makes representations to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) who comes from the area, and he indicates justifiable concern. Mr. Speaker, every year parliament goes through this same process and deals with this same kind of measure. About the only difference in the script is the amount of money involved. Every year we put up with the spectacle of the parliament of Canada bailing out the CNR from under debt charges that it

December 2, 1969
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada should not be expected to carry. When the Canadian National Railways system was formed in 1923, and ever since, the deck has been stacked against it in favour of the economic pirates who promoted and invested in several railways that subsequently went belly up. The deck has been stacked to make sure that those people are paid off. They have been but the people of Canada have been paying ever since, and are still paying.
Some sizeable part of the money provided by this bill is for the payment of a deficit resulting from the interest that has been charged the CNR on this debt in the past year. Much of that debt is a result of the financing and refinancing of the Canadian National Railways system since 1923. When the Grand Trunk Railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern, probably the three main railways, were going bankrupt they were formed into the CNR system. Their indebtedness was taken over by the Canadian National Railways system, and in the years since the Canadian National Railways and the Parliament of Canada have been paying, paying and paying. This suits very well the people who do not like publicly owned enterprises of any kind and in particular do not like a publicly owned railway system. Since 1923 it has suited their purpose to hold up the Canadian National Railways system as a terrible example of how public ownership does not work and how private ownership is holy, pure, successful, efficient and so on. The myth has been perpetrated and perpetuated by these free enterprise opponents of publicly owned enterprise that the CNR somehow is bad because it always loses money and is publicly owned.
The facts are otherwise. The Canadian National Railways system in most years has shown operating profits. In 17 of the last 24 years it has shown a railway operating profit. In 21 of the last 24 years, after considering income from other operations such as hotels and telegraph services, it has shown an operating profit. Of the last 24 years only in the years 1958, 1960 and 1962 was there a loss on the Canadian National Railways system. One could become involved in unkind partisan arguments by trying to make a case that this might have had a relationship to the government of the day, but I shall not do that. I think it had to do mostly with the type of debt load with which the CNR has had to contend since 1923. I should like to quote from the Winnipeg Tribune of April 25 last. This article points out the following:

The CNR made an operating profit of about $41,000,000, in 1968, its annual report disclosed Thursday, but its accountants had to use red ink once more because of the debt burden that goes back to the founding of the nationally-owned railway in 1923.
This report points out that the net income, before interest on the debt, was $41,274,438 but that the interest on the debt was $70,450,968. This means that parliament must vote another $29,176,530 to wipe out that interest debt. The article continued:
The CNR carries a burden of fixed-charge debt inherited from the several bankrupt railways whose operations it took over when it was formed. As of last Dec. 31, its total long-term debt was $1,919,560,709, including bonds amounting to $1,132,903,264.
So long as the Canadian National Railways system is required by this Parliament to operate under such conditions it can never operate efficiently and can never provide an effective transportation service for the Canadian people. So long as this system of ours is expected to operate under these conditions, it must continue to fight a losing battle in attempting to remain a healthy and viable operation. As it loses its viability, it automatically decreases the service it can provide to the Canadian people.
The operating statements of the Canadian National Railways over the past 24 years I believe indicate that there has been efficient management in the face of these debts, that there have been competent employees and that a massive effort has been made to succeed in operating the Canadian National Railways system in the face of the horrendous obstacles this parliament has continually placed before it. I mentioned earlier that in only three of the last 24 years has the system shown an operating loss. In all the other 21 years there has been an operating profit. It is very interesting to note that the peak period in respect of number of employees was in the year 1952 when there were 131,297 employees. Today, there are 85,240 employees, some 46,000 fewer. I submit that this says something pretty good about their productivity and competence in operating our nationally owned railway system.
In spite of having 46,000 fewer employees, the railway has a larger amount of freight ton mile revenue and other kinds of revenue than it ever had before. The issue of passenger business is confronting members of this House and the people of Canada as a result of applications by both railways to further decrease their passenger services. Even in this area, however, the Canadian National Rail-
December 2, 1969	COMMONS
ways system, I submit, has made a very good effort in the face again of great obstacles at a time when all other private railway carriers in North America have thrown up their hands in despair. Back in the period 1944-45, the Canadian National Railways system was operating some 3,338,000 revenue passenger miles. By 1962 this figure had dropped to a low point of 1,044,000 revenue passenger miles. In the face of that, the CNR did not give up. It began a program of modernization and expansion of passenger operations by means of publicizing and persuading the public to use railway transportation.

Since that low point in 1962, the number of revenue passenger miles has climbed to 2,046,000, equivalent to the kind of passenger business the company was doing in 1947. Admittedly, costs are a great deal higher now than they were then, but the evidence is conclusive that the company has made a conscientious and consistent effort to regain and restore passenger service to something near former levels in this country. I submit that the management and the employees of that nationally-owned transportation company deserve the thanks and the compliments of the House and of the people of Canada.
They have a long road before them yet. Many more improvements and developments are needed in the passenger service as well as in all other aspects of railroading, but at least they have been trying, which is much more than can be said for their main competitor, the Canadian Pacific Railway. Our publicly owned national railway system has never had a fair chance to operate successfully. It has been and still is burdened with a debt load that prevents it from paying an investment return to the people of Canada and, even more important, that prevents it from doing an even better job in providing service. We have been lucky that this company has done as well as it has. The previous and present management and employees are to be congratulated. No privately owned system could operate under the same debt burden as has the CNR. If a privately owned system tried, it would have been bankrupt a long time ago.
While the CNR and the people of Canada continue to pay and pay dearly, its competitor, the CPR thrives on gifts from the people of Canada which, since 1881, have returned dividends to this corporation and its shareholders amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars. I think one could safely say they have

Governments of Canada since 1923, when the CNR was set up, have been refinancing the national railway in various ways such as buying up bonds and advancing funds. They have always done it in such a way as to completely safeguard the interests of the original investors of the bankrupt railways. Those who had investments in the old Grand Trunk Railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Canadian Northern Railways have all received the full return on their moneys. None of them is still alive but the railways are still paying. I suspect that the original investments have been repaid two or three times over and we are still paying.
Contrast that with the attitude of this and of previous Canadian governments to their own employees. The government and the CNR management-and here I must be somewhat critical of the CNR management-have always been able to find ways of persuading this Parliament to provide moneys for such things as equipment and for buying up old bonds. However, they have not been able to devise a way whereby some money could be included in Bill C-7 or in previous bills of this kind to do something about the pensions of retired CNR employees. Whether there is only one of them or one million, the fact that we would require formal loyal employees of ours to exist on the kind of pensions that some are now receiving is something of which all in this chamber should be ashamed.
As of October 7 last year, in a return filed in answer to a question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), there were, believe it or not, 388 retired CNR employees receiving less than $25 a month. There were another 639 receiving between $25 and $29 a month. There were another 1,301 receiving between $30 and $39 a month. There were another 1,062 receiving between $40 and $49 a month, and until one arrives at the figure of $99.99 a month there is a total of 7,715 retired CNR employees receiving less than $100 a month as pension. I know of the case of a man who served the CNR for over 30 years who is receiving a pension of less than $35 because his service was interrupted as a result of illness. His pension benefits did not accrue until after he started working for the CNR the second time.

Every time this situation is mentioned, government members, both in the Transport Committee and in the House, agree that it is terrible. They express all kinds of sympathy and support for the idea of doing something to increase the pensions of retired CNR employees. Every minister who has ever piloted this kind of bill through the House has, at some time or other, expressed sympathy and deplored the situation, but none of them has yet brought anything to this House to deal with the matter. The CNR officials are equally vociferous in expressing their sympathy and in saying how badly they feel about it. They even promised to seriously consider ways of dealing with this matter by raising the pensions of retired CNR employees. In the Transport Committee last spring the President of the CNR, in answer to my question, promised to give serious thought to this matter. On July 29 I wrote him, and two days later I received an acknowledgment from his executive assistant. I have not heard a word from him since. It does not matter if he does not write to me, but it does matter that he should do something about the over 7,000 retired CNR employees.
Surely this is a problem that should be solved, and provision should be made in this bill for solving it. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would then not have to hound the government on this subject. He would have more time to hound them on other subjects on which action has been equally long delayed.
May I say something more about CNR financing and ask hon. members to look at the pension trust funds held by the CNR. According to the company's annual report there is supposed to be $1,414,744,000 in that fund, but there is only $743 million in it. Where is the rest of the employees' pension money? The difference of $671,423,250 is owing by the CNR to the employees pension trust fund. I do not really blame the CNR for being in that situation. I suspect that in past years they have been desperate for operating funds and that when the railway system was putting up the majority of the money for pension funds they had no other choice but to use the money for railway operations.
In 1967, provision was made for the CNR to commence repaying the $671 million to the pension trust fund. So, during 1967 and 1968 they repaid with interest, slightly over $3 million. Mr. Speaker, the Company have allowed themselves 60 years to repay this $675 million. They are fairly safe in doing

that, since it is hardly likely that all the employees of the railway would retire at once.

But surely this is a misuse of trust funds. That misuse has been caused by successive governments of Canada and successive Parliaments keeping the Canadian National Railways system continually burdened with a load of debt they cannot possibly get out from under, a burden of debt that originated with bankrupt corporate pirates who put on Canada's back railway systems that were not paying. Mr. Speaker, in the financial statement of the Canadian National Railways system this Pension liability is listed as an unfunded liability. All that really means is that the money is not in the pension trust fund. It is accountants' gobbledy-gook, and in fact what it means is that in the past this publicly owned railway system had to use their employees' pension money for other purposes.
The time has long past for members in all parties in this House to resist the passage of this bill until the government finally-after 100 years of governments that refused to come up with a national transportation policy-comes up with a transportation policy that is meaningful and purposeful in the interests of the Canadian people rather than in the interests of the bond holders and the shareholders, many of whom do not live here.
We must resist this business of being asked year after year to vote money when we have no clear picture as to where we are going in this country in terms of transportation policy.
Those words are a direct quote from a speech made by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). To some degree I must disagree with him because I think we have had a clear picture, as clear as mud. We have had transportation policies the first purpose of which was to give great profits to a few while the public paid and paid, and rail services went through a pattern of deterioration that no self-respecting country would tolerate.
We have had policies that allowed the privately owned CPR system to be almost a law unto itself. We have had policies that have continually hamstrung and stopped our own national railway system from operating efficiently in the best interests of the people of this country. This Parliament must come to grips with the whole matter of public rather
December 2, 1969	COMMONS
than private ownership of our railway systems. Surely, there is sufficient evidence now to convince even the most ardent opponent of public ownership that the private sector, in this particular industry at least, has failed Canada, has not acted in the best interests of the Canadian people, and has lost any right or privilege it had to operate a railway system in this nation.
The time has long past for this Parliament to enact legislation nationalizing the CPR system and merging it with our publicly owned national railway system to operate a national, efficient, effective rail transportation network throughout the entire nation. We could do it on a scale of efficiency and service which would be the envy of any other nation in the world. I, for one, Mr. Speaker, am in no hurry to see this bill pass. I hope that members on both sides of the House will agree that the bill should be held up until such time as we get at least two commitments from the government and the management of the Canadian National Railways system.
The first commitment should be that the government and the CNR management will bring in a measure in the next session of this parliament to provide for an increase in the pensions of retired CNR employees. The second commitment should be that the government will bring in measures in the next session of this Parliament that will relieve the Canadian National system of at least the long-term debt which amounts to $1.9 billion; in other words, that this be written off the books. We do not want any more of those half-made commitments, "Yes, we are going to consider it seriously," and "Yes, we will announce it in due time as government policy," for that will take too many years.
Most of this debt consists of money now owing by the CNR to the people of Canada as a result of advances and loans. In fact, there were a couple of hundred million dollar interest free loans. Further, Mr. Speaker, I think that the measure should include a grant totalling $675 million to allow for the full refunding of the CNR employees' pension fund. The $1.9 billion plus the $675 million would, for the first time, give the CNR a chance to operate efficiently and effectively, and would lift from its back this burden of debt which was none of its fault. This course would allow the publicly owned system to show the privately owned operators how to run a railway, once it was free of this debt that the management could never repay even if they lived 1000 years.

Surely, with one passenger train in that area such a system is hardly required; it could easily be fitted in with the freight train schedule. If the line is to be kept open a certain amount of upgrading of the roadbed must take place in any case and in the meantime the trains could take it a little more slowly. We have shown by the proposed schedules that the train could go through that area and still save time, even with poor roadbeds in certain parts of the north country.
For some time now, Mr. Speaker, we have been hearing a great deal about the development of Northern Ontario and how to encourage people to live there. This year the government passed a bill to encourage new industries to open in the area and have given incentive grants. But how can we expect people to come if we offer poor transportation services? Just about a month after a program was started to encourage people to move north, the railroad stated that it wished to cancel the existing inadequate service.
I believe that a transportation system properly run and managed should not lose money. This is borne out by the action of the courageous gentleman in Barrie who ran a special train to Toronto and made money. It seems to me that these losses indicate poor management and we, who represent the people of Canada, should examine that aspect a little more closely. I believe that the board of the CNR should include members who are elected by the people. What is wrong with putting a member of Parliament on the board of a Crown corporation? It has been done elsewhere; but we, in Ottawa, always seem to shy away from the idea. Yet, when we ask a minister in the House a question about a Crown corporation, the first thing we hear is that Crown corporations are independent,
DEBATES	1495
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada that they must run their own affairs and that we cannot interfere. It is the system that is wrong and that is why I take to task the previous hon. member who spoke about this government not taking its responsibilities seriously. I do not care whether a Liberal, Tory or NDP government is in power, so long as the present system exists we shall not be able to control the CNR or any other Crown corporation. We should decide, therefor, that there must be more representatives of the people on the boards of those corporations. That is why I advocate a member of Parliament being a representative on Crown Boards and agencies. Are we that stupid that we are not capable of serving on such boards? Of course, many public servants think we are stupid; we are treated with contempt by many of them.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
But I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that on some boards the government has formed, and the National Arts Centre is a case in point, there is not one member who is as highly qualified to serve as several hon. members in this House. So far as the CNR is concerned, the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner) who sits behind me in the House and who has had several years service with the CNR probably knows more about the CNR and matters of transportation than any member of the present board of directors of the CNR. Certainly, there is no reason in the world why members of this House should not serve on the boards of Crown corporations. That is why I feel that until this House decides that we must have greater control over the way people's money is spent, we shall continue to be confronted with the same difficulty.
The hon. member who preceded me spoke of holding up this bill because year after year we must approve the allocation of a certain amount of money. It is true that we go through this every year and that is futile, but we shall not get anywhere by refusing to pass the bill because the railway must continue to operate. It is the system that must be changed, and there is only one way to change it. We ought to change it right here in this House so that hon. members of this House may serve on the boards of directors of Crown corporations.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS, AIR CANADA PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when he introduced this bill on November 13, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gray) told us that a similar bill to
December 2, 1989
1496	COMMONS DEBATES
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada appropriate funds for the CNR and Air Canada has come before Parliament year after year, the exception being those two years that were combined. I believe an hon. member who preceded me said that this has been going on for 45 years. I do not know whether that is quite accurate, but the mere fact that we have been doing something for 45 years does not mean that we are going about it the right way. I join with many spokesmen on this side of the House who have complained about this being a useless exercise. Here we are being asked to approve the granting of some $200 million already spent. What is the good of this? What if we say that we will not grant the money? It has been spent. We are also asked to approve another $82 million, I believe, to be spent between January and July 1, 1970 for obligations incurred prior to January, 1967. In other words, that $82 million is also committed. This, I feel, is the most unbusinesslike way of handling finances that I have ever run across. Although we cannot do anything about the money that has been spent, I feel that we should demand some accounting so that if these moneys are requested, in future years at least we will have some idea what these corporations are doing with the money. But here we are presented with a fait accompli; the money is spent and we cannot do anything about it now. I think each and every one of us should examine these items closely in committee to make sure the money has been spent properly, so that in future years we may have some basis for a decision.
In this modern day and age nothing is more important to a country like ours than transportation, and it certainly behooves us to know what the government plans to do. Does it have a comprehensive transportation scheme? Does it have a plan to hook up outlying parts of Canada with the centre, provide passenger service and provide for the movement of freight? I say this afternoon that despite all the committees the government appointed, despite all the reports that have been brought in about the Atlantic area and other areas, the entire subject of transportation today lies in greater confusion than ever before.
Although I was not a member of this House in 1967 when the National Transportation Act was introduced, I read many of the pertinent debates and speeches of opposition spokesmen. Many of those spokesmen are in the House today. I agree with many of the objections raised at that time by the opposition.

Government supporters contended the act would be the be-all and end-all for transportation. There we were, setting up the board under this czar, this renowned expert on transport who would immediately solve all our difficulties. I say that if the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) is complaining about members of Parliament not having anything to do with the operation of the CNR he ought to point his finger at the government which brought in the National Transportation Act, because the Act makes it impossible for the ordinary member of Parliament or any other person to question the activities of the CNR. That is where the blame lies.
Some of the confusion the National Transportation Act created has been much in evidence recently, as shown by the recent unprecedented action by the Air Traffic Association of Canada. That body, in a unanimous vote, condemned the Air Traffic Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission for its absolute failure to come up with any workable and enforceable air traffic regulations. Here is a body set up to devise a system of control now telling us, in effect, "The regulations are not workable or enforceable, and therefore are not being enforced". In other words, carriers are running rampant and not paying attention to schedules or regulations. In this area the CTC has fallen down completely.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Again, let me cite as evidence what happened at the recent meeting in Toronto of the Automotive Transport Association of Ontario. Here we have a body composed of the operators of probably one of the fastest growing segments of our transport system. Here again, we find a body harshly condemning the Canadian Transport Commission for failure to act in their area. These people say in effect that because the government has failed to announce its intentions with regard to implementing Part III of the Transport Act, a rash of provincial regulations has sprung up which is crippling the work of the association. I am pleased to hear that these people are meeting in Ottawa today and I hope the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) will be able to make an announcement to the House soon with regard to Part III of the act.
The failure of the Canadian Transport Commission to operate effectively is underlined by the recent action on the part of the railway companies in applying for the abandonment of some 31 passenger trains. I shall not discuss the details of these applications-
December 2, 1989	COMMONS
that is the job of the Transport Commission- but I do wish to point out that these applications for permission to abandon passenger service have caused a great deal of worry and concern in many areas of Canada.
By way of illustration I should like to read into the record a letter from the President of the Moncton Board of Trade addressed to Mr. D. H. Jones, Chairman of the railway transport committee of the Canadian Transport Commission. It states:
Dear Mr. Jones:
The Moncton Board of Trade were shocked to read news reports last week that The Canadian National Railway has filed application to discontinue passenger rail service between Saint John and Moncton. We feel that this service is a most important link between two of Atlantic Canada's major cities and in some weather conditions the only reasonable means of travel. We are also concerned that discontinuance of this service will seriously inconvenience many Canadians living between Moncton and Saint John who use this means of transportation to travel to our City and to Saint John to do their shopping.
The letter goes on to say:
We feel this idea is particular folly at a time when the federal and provincial governments are taking action and spending a great deal of funds to develop Canada's Atlantic region.
Because I was concerned about this facet of the procedure I asked the Minister of Transport in the House one day last week what he intended to do in response to this proposal by the railways which would effectively destroy any attempt by his colleague the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) to build up industry and improve employment prospects in that region. The minister replied that he would do what he could to prevent any such action taking place. I hope the Minister of Transport was sincere and that he will exert every effort to ensure that employment prospects are not cut down because of unilateral proposals on the part of the railways.
The letter continues:
Although we as businessmen understand the CNR's concern about continuing a service that is losing money, we also realise that all businesses, particularly in the service and transportation industries, have to provide some services which may not be as profitable as others. We feel this route is one such service that our national railway must be prepared to provide in the public interest along with its other routes that are profitable.
This letter expresses the concern felt among the business community. The labour community shares this anxiety. Railway workers, in particular, are upset; they do not know when their jobs will end; they do not know which lines will be discontinued. I
DEBATES	1497
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada received a telegram from one of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen locals expressing concern about the probable loss of jobs following the abandonment or curtailment of passenger services. I was in touch with the sender of this telegram recently, and after talking the situation over I believe I can assure him that the loss of jobs will not be as severe as he fears. Here, I give full marks to the CNR; they are doing everything they can to cushion the impact of the action which the company has proposed.
I cannot go along with those who are always ready and willing to take a swipe at the CNR. In this connection I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Regina Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). In my opinion, he stated the position very well and very clearly.
I feel that in the past few years the CNR has made every effort to modernize its system, and done everything it could to introduce businesslike methods. It has computerized a large part of its operations, introduced new types of services, and so on. I honestly believe the CNR is making a real, one hundred per cent effort to keep going. I say again that the blame for the present unsettled situation rests clearly with the Canadian Transport Commission.
Here before me is an act drawn up in 1967 which states that all transportation services in the country should be compensatory; that if it can be shown that the railways are losing money, and if it is proved that these services are essential, the companies can be subsidized up to 80 per cent. To my mind this is nothing but a licence to steal. Can you blame the railways if they juggle their figures a bit when they have been told that if they can show a loss they will get subsidies up to 80 per cent? Would it not have been much better and more sensible to have written a provision into the act to the effect that the railways must produce their costs for inspection by the railway transport committee of the CTC? Then, if subsidies are in order, let them be granted. Why throw the people of Canada into a state of anxiety because the railways are encouraged to follow the stupid method of making a blanket application to abandon every passenger line in the country? No wonder business is upset. No wonder people are worried.
The fact that the applications have been made cannot be changed now. This is the procedure which has been provided in the act. I for one do not believe for a moment that the CNR has any hope or any intention

December 2, 1969
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada of abandoning all its passenger services. I am thoroughly convinced this action was taken in the hope that these services would be declared essential and would therefore be subsidized. But the applications have been made; the damage has been done. Now, it is up to the CTC to act, and to act quickly. If, as an hon. member has suggested, there has been any monkeying with the books, if some of the costing procedures of the CNR are not satisfactory, let the CTC examine this aspect of the applications and make its findings known. If the figures are not satisfactory, let the committee tell the railway it must continue to operate these services. If, on the other hand, the CTC is satisfied that the figures are correct, that the lines are losing money and that the services are essential, let the government provide a subsidy to the CNR. But by all means keep the services going and let us get this whole situation resolved.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I was pleased to pick up a copy of the speech which Mr. Pickersgill delivered this morning to the Canadian Association of Movers. The Movers Association is mainly interested in Part III of the National Transportation Act, but fortunately Mr. Pickersgill recognizes the seriousness of these rail passenger applications and he took the time to talk to the Association about the various applications. In the course of his speech he pointed out that a section of the National Transportation Act provided that the railways should not be obliged to carry the burden of operating uneconomic services, but that this did not mean, as some people have construed, that all of the trains involved would automatically be discontinued. Then, Mr. Pickersgill went on to say:
The act places on the Canadian Transport Commission the responsibility of deciding whether a particular service is not required in the public interest and therefore should be discontinued or whether the public need requires that it be kept in operation-with compensation.
In other words, at public expense. Then, he went on to say something that I think should be on the record:
In essence, what the Commission must do in each case is to weigh the public need against the amount that the public treasury would be required to pay in order to continue the service. There are some obvious cases where passenger train service is going to have to be continued because no other alternative mode of transportation is available in the area. On the other hand, there are some services where train patronage has all but disappeared and there is no apparent justification for the use of public funds to support something the public clearly does not want.

I think this emphasizes something that some people are not too willing to recognize. I do not think it fair to ask any carrier to continue a service which people are not using if an alternative mode of transportation is available. We must be reasonable about these things. We should not damage our case by demanding that all routes be subsidized holus bolus.
Mr. Pickersgill then went on to clarify the position regarding appeals, something that the hon. member for St. John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) dealt with when he spoke a couple of weeks ago. While he did not say in so many words that an appeal rests in every case, Mr. Pickersgill pointed out that although the Act does not provide that hearings take place in public, his own layman's interpretation of the Act-and knowing Mr. Pickersgill, I would say his interpretation is the law-is that its provisions are very close to being mandatory on this point.
People, particularly in my area, are demanding these hearings be held. Naturally, they do not want to lose passenger services, though they recognize that some may have to go. But what they do want is some statement of policy by the government or the Canadian Transport Commission, or by somebody in authority, regarding these applications for abandonment.
Although these applications were filed almost two months ago, the railways are still waiting for an indication from the CTC when these applications will be heard. In the meantime, people are wondering what is going to happen. Just like a snowball rolling downhill, rumours are starting to fly. First of all 50 people are going to be laid off; this figure grows to 100 and then to 200. Then, it is rumoured that all these services will be discontinued. The Minister of Transport should take the lead in getting the Canadian Transport Commission to take action on these applications without further delay.
The people in the Atlantic provinces are still waiting for some clear statement of policy from the government. The Minister of Transport tells the House one thing; then he goes to a public meeting and makes a different statement. For example, he told this House that the freeze on freight rates would remain until such time as a complete overhaul of transportation policy for the mari-times had been made. Then, we hardly have time to get home and read the newspapers before the minister has announced that the
December 2, 1969

freeze has been lifted. How can we in the Atlantic provinces have any faith in the statements of this government?
An editorial in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal in October, 1969, dealt with the effect of this action on the region in an article headed "Erratic rates harm region". The article commences:
No businessman in the Atlantic provinces has the least idea from one day to the next how much it is going to cost to bring raw materials in or ship products out.
The editorial points out that freight rates which had been frozen for two and a half years to allow this government to develop a transportation policy for the maritimes had suddenly been lifted. As a result, railway freight rates shot up 9 to 18 per cent at once, and they are expected to go higher in the immediate future.
There has also been confusion over the railway's announcement that it would cancel rates on less than carload lots and bring in higher express rates for the area. I must give the Minister of Transport credit: On this occasion he acted promptly and the railways deferred action. The minister then went on to refer to the federal-provincial committee and intimated the committee might recommend removal of some of the subsidies in the area, though did not say whether the subsidies were on lumber, fish or potato shipments. As a result, no shipper in the area knows whether to expect 20 per cent higher freight costs or 40 per cent. In fact, they have no idea what is coming next.
The editorial to which I have referred concludes with this paragraph:
We need a new transportation policy, without a doubt. The rest of Canada got a new deal in March, 1967, and this region was promised one at that time.
The latest blow to this region, though all parts of Canada will feel the impact, is the announcement made by the express carriers, including not only rail but air carriers, that as of December 1 shipments of flowers and horticultural products will be accepted only if the consignors assume all risk of loss or damage from frost. This may seem a minor item, but to the florists, of whom there are a great many in this country, it is a very serious blow. In most regions in the Atlantic provinces the only way to ship such products is by express freight. In effect, the express carriers are telling these producers that all shipments will be made at their own risk.
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada
I am sure the House can see the possibilities that can arise here. According to an editorial I have here, if the railway is entirely freed from responsibility for frost damage to these shipments, any concern to prevent such loss will largely evaporate. Wide open exemption invites careless handling. In other words, why worry too much about these products if you are not responsible for their loss anyway?
I lay the blame for this situation on the railways, and I suggest the Minister of Transport take immediate action to correct it. When he was replying to a question in the House on Friday, I was pleased to hear the minister say that a meeting was being held on Monday in Ottawa with the parties concerned and that he was hopeful the matter would be resolved. No announcement has been made in the House so far, but perhaps we will hear either today or tomorrow that the Minister of Transport has taken action to correct the situation. Although this problem is faced by the whole of Canada, I speak for the Atlantic region since I am naturally more familiar with that area than the rest of the country.
The blame for not introducing a transportation policy in the maritimes rests squarely on the government, and on the Canadian Transport Commission, which is a creature of the government. I submit action must be taken immediately to develop once and for all a clear and comprehensive transportation policy for the Atlantic region.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
In so far as Air Canada is concerned, I have no great complaint, although again I complain about this method of financing. I think we have a government service which is one of the best in the world. It has been recognized as such and we rightly should be proud of it. In some areas the service could be improved. I feel that interregional traffic, for example, could be better handled than it is at the present time. The whole system of scheduling should be revised.
Perhaps I am bearing a personal cross here because I am thinking particularly of my own experience. The flight leaves Moncton for Montreal and lands at Montreal airport half an hour after the Ottawa flight has left. This means that a traveller has to stay at the Montreal airport for two hours waiting for the next flight. It seems ridiculous that this jet flight from Toronto to Montreal to Moncton, which arrives at 11 o'clock in the morning at
1500	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada Moncton, should sit for an hour and thirty-five minutes, to my knowledge not being serviced other than refuelled, then head back to Saint John and Montreal, arriving after the Ottawa flight has left. Why could the flight not be scheduled to connect with the plane coming in from Sept-Iles? It could be set back half an hour and connect with the scheduled flight from Moncton. You would then have a connection.
These are some of the things people are complaining about in respect of Air Canada. They have in mind the intercity service between Halifax and Moncton, two of the largest centres in this area. There are only two flights from Halifax. You leave there at 8:30 or 9 and there is no other flight until eleven o'clock. All that is involved is a revision of the schedule to fit what people want and will use.
Before we give this bill second reading, I invite other members of the House to state their views. I feel it should be examined very closely and carefully by the committee. There are many things that should be corrected in the future, and until such time as the committee is able to give these things careful consideration we will never have a proper and comprehensive transportation policy in this country.

The Canadian National Railways has a certain way of putting things to our Canadian citizens. We have to run around like crazy rats to find out what is going on in CN administration. Still, we do not get any answers from anyone.
The press release continues:
Mr. Roberts said that CN's passenger policy remains unchanged-"to eliminate the passenger deficit, not the passenger business."
Mr. Roberts is general manager of passenger sales and services. I cannot explain this statement and 1 am sure the CN cannot explain it either. that Bill C-15, to amend the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act (Age Discrimination), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-15 which is being presented this afternoon is an act to amend the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act regarding age discrimination. The chief purpose of the bill is to add age discrimination to the list of prohibited employment practices unless age is a bona fide occupational qualification. A secondary purpose is to prohibit the employer from including in an employment application form, advertisement or written or oral inquiry, a question or request for particulars as to the applicant's race, national origin, colour, religion or age unless by reason of a bona fide occupational qualification.
Under clause 1, the present section 4 is amended by adding, where necessary, the words "or age unless age is a bona fide occupational qualification." I would ask hon. members to support this measure, and I would ask members of the government party to permit the measure to go to committee. It is of particular importance at this time. It has always been of importance, but the need for such an amendment is becoming more and more obvious.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
DEBATES	December 2, 1989
Of course, one of the reasons is the government's policy of creating unemployment in an effort to control inflation, in my opinion a rather shortsighted approach which will not solve inflation problems but will create great hardship for many of our people. In a situation of this type, it is frequently the older worker who suffers the most. It is frequently the worker who needs employment the most who is placed at a disadvantage.
To my way of thinking another important reason is regional mobility. It is becoming obvious that some sections of the country are not able to sustain their present populations. Government policies of regional development have proven inadequate to the task, and many workers have to move from their areas of birth to new areas. This kind of regional mobility is most difficult for the older worker. Perhaps I should define what I mean by an older worker. We are not talking about somebody who is 70 years of age. Today, it seems that if one is over the age of 45 years one is subject to discrimination, except of course if one is trying to become the Prime Minister of Canada.
One of the great difficulties encountered by older workers moving from one area to another, aside from employment, is the problem of obtaining housing. Frequently their age works against the possibility of their obtaining mortgages. In every way, faced with this problem of mobility, the older worker finds himself in great difficulty.
Because of the rapid increase in technology people over the age of 45 years find that the skills they laboriously acquired through then-apprenticeship, through their earlier years of training and practice, are becoming obsolete. Unfortunately, some of our manpower retraining programs do not adequately provide training opportunities and encouragement for the older worker.
One of the major problems is psychological. From my experience, and from the experience of many other people, it has been found that the older worker is a very desirable worker. Many employers have found that older workers have a great deal to offer. They have experience. They have reduced family commitments. They have reliability. They have a greater accuracy. In many cases they have greater stamina. Their continuity on the job is better than that of younger workers. They are more willing to accept shift work, and to accept training. Why then is it so difficult for some of our older workers to find employment? As I stated earlier, the problem is largely psychological.
December 2, 1969

This country and many others seem to be on a youth kick. In other words, whatever is young seems good, and if it is a little old it is not so good. It is one of the great fallacies of our time that youth, efficiency and knowledge are equated. Obviously this is not always the case. There are many desirable aspects to youth, and also many desirable aspects to those no longer young. Therefore, it is a psychological barrier that we must overcome.. I think that an amendment to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act would go a long way toward overcoming the psychological barrier.
It may be that even this attempt through Bill C-15 to have that act amended in order to overcome the psychological barrier, and to bring in legal sanctions against those who practise discrimination because of age, may not be sufficient. In the past the government has tried to bring in programs to encourage the hiring of older workers. Unfortunately, those programs did not work. They were not effective. For a number of reasons which have never been carefully explained they fell far short of their objective.
A considerable sum of money was made available to employers if they would hire older workers. That sum of money was never used up, and many older workers were not hired. Fortunately for many of our people, particularly those who are in trade unions, there is protection under seniority rights. But for those who are not in unions, age can be a severe problem. As things stand now they do not have this protection under the law, except in some provinces. There are some provinces that offer this protection, but older workers do not have this protection in federal law, and as a result older workers are sometimes left at the mercy of their employers.
Even in the case of trade unions where there are seniority rights, problems occur over which the unions have no control. For instance, when a plant closes down and a man who has been working in it for 20 or 30 years is released his seniority is gone. He has to start all over again at the bottom and sometimes it is difficult for him to make that kind of adjustment.
Even in union shops work practices change. Because of changing technology in a plant, people are shifted and the older worker is placed at a disadvantage. What we are seeing is what some employers consider a private benefit to themselves. They seem to feel, despite evidence to the contrary, that older

Fair Employment Practices Act workers are not desirable. As a result, society generally has to pick up the cost through unemployment insurance or welfare programs of some kind or another. I think this is one of the things which must change. It is one of the areas where the government will have to bring in measures, and go beyond what I am suggesting in my bill, to see that every factory in this country is required to have a certain percentage of its employees over a certain age. It might not be enough to accept the provisions of this bill, although I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is a necessary start. The provisions of the bill would at least assist in this direction and would certainly enable us to look forward to the day when everyone accepts the necessity of ensuring equal opportunity to people beyond the age of youth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act which came into effect on July 1, 1953, is designed to prevent and eliminate practices of discrimination against persons in regard to employment and in regard to membership in a trade union because of race, national origin, colour or religion. The Liberal government of the day under the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent in proposing the Act was translating into law a basic principle of human rights. As a member of various international organizations, Canada in recent years has subscribed to general declarations

DEBATES	December 2, 1969
of the basic rights and liberties of the individual. For instance, Canada accepted the United Nations Charter and Declaration of Human Rights, and the Declaration of Aims of the International Labour Organizations. Among the declarations of rights was one that the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act is designed to protect-the right of equality of opportunity in employment.
It is recognized that legislation alone does not entirely change the attitudes of mind which are at the root of discrimination, and the need for continued public and private educational efforts to do away with prejudice and ignorance is unfortunately very apparent. Like other federal legislation in the labour field, the act applies only to works and businesses within federal jurisdiction. These, of course, include navigation, shipping, railways, canals, telegraphs, aerodromes, airlines, radio and television broadcasting, banks and federal Crown corporations. However, like most federal labour legislation, it has had a far-reaching influence on the labour legislation of all the provinces in our country and now all ten provinces have passed similar legislation covering works and businesses within their jurisdictions.
The act states that no employer shall refuse to employ, or continue to employ, or otherwise discriminate against any person in regard to employment, or any term or condition of employment, because of his race, national origin, colour or religion. Further, an employer is not to use any employment agency which practices discrimination against persons seeking employment. Employers are not to make written or oral inquiries or use application forms relating to employment which express directly or indirectly any limitation, specification or preference based on race, national origin, colour or religion except where based on a bona fide occupational qualification. There are similar provisions against discriminatory advertising.
The act also forbids discriminatory actions by labour unions. No labour union may exclude anyone from full membership, or expel, suspend or otherwise discriminate against anyone in regard to his employment because of race, colour, national origin or religion. The act does not apply to employers of fewer than five employees, and it excludes non-profit, educational, charitable, fraternal, religious and social organizations.
While the legislation lays down penalties for positive acts of discrimination, it is
December 2, 1969	COMMONS
expected that most of the cases which arise will be settled by conciliation without any need for recourse to the courts. Experience with similar legislation in other places shows that the existence of the legislation alone is sufficient, in many cases, to prevent discrimination. Then, too, it is likely that many cases of discrimination will be found to have been caused by misunderstanding or thoughtlessness on the part of one or both of the parties, and that in such cases complaints can be ironed out without difficulty.
However, under the act a person who feels he has been discriminated against may make a complaint in writing to the director, Fair Employment Practices Branch, Canada Department of Labour, Ottawa. An officer of that branch will be directed to inquire immediately into the complaint and try to bring about a satisfactory settlement. Most complaints are settled at that stage. However, if a complaint is not satisfactorily settled, the Minister of Labour is empowered to set up an industrial inquiry commission to investigate the circumstances and to make recommendations to the minister as to how it can best be settled. The minister can then issue any order he considers necessary to carry out the recommendations of the commission, and such orders are final and binding on the parties. The act also provides for prosecution by way of summary proceedings in the courts, with the consent in writing of the minister, against anyone who does anything prohibited by the act or refuses or neglects to do anything required by it.
The experience of the federal government in the administration of this act has been, in general, most satisfactory. During the past fiscal year ending March 31, 1969, some 73 complaints were received by the Fair Employment Practices Branch. Of these, 47 related to discrimination in employment. All were processed satisfactorily and settled.
Our Department of Labour has received the fullest co-operation from the various trade union and human rights committees including the National Committee on Human Rights of the Canadian Labour Congress, from employer groups and from the voluntary agencies in the human rights field, as well as from the press, radio and television. The Department of Labour has expended a great deal of effort in the educational field in encouraging fair employment practices. In this connection, members of the House may recall the department's recent newspaper advertising which

Fair Employment Practices Act apparently made a few people uncomfortable but was generally well received across the country.
In addition to investigating complaints, the Fair Employment Practices Branch of the department is actively promoting the principle of affirmative action, not just the elimination of discriminatory practices per se but positive steps to encourage members of badly disadvantaged minority groups to take training and come forward for employment. This promotion is being directed at management, union and government agencies at all levels.
The branch publishes and distributes pamphlets and posters on the subject, produces items for television spots, posters and exhibits, and encourages or participates in radio and television discussions. Several hundred thousand pieces of literature on the laws and the roots of prejudice have been distributed during the past year. The Department of Labour also advertises the provisions of the act in the foreign language press of Canada, and prepares articles for other papers and journals. Officers of the department attend regional, national and international conferences on discrimination in employment. During the past year they made more than 60 addresses to labour conventions and to meetings where management was broadly represented. Over the years the federal Department of Labour has been widely commended for its work in this field, and rightly so.
However-and this point was mentioned by the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Hopkins)-successful experience with the administration of this act has not made the department self-satisfied or insensitive to the possibilities of improving the legislation, its administration, or the associated work of education and persuasion. Indeed, at the request of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) a group of officers in his department have in recent months been examining ways and means of enhancing the value of the act by broadening its coverage and increasing its effectiveness. Among other things, they are considering the possibility of extending the current prohibitions to discrimination based on age.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The December, 1968, issue of the magazine "Monetary Times" has an interesting article at page 23 headed "Prejudice and Discrimination". The article comments on a recent study by Dr. Edro Signori, a psychology professor at the University of British Columbia, on dis-
December 2, 19G9

Fair Employment Practices Act criminatory beliefs and attitudes toward employment by socially disadvantaged groups. Dr. Signori and his assistants have studied 400 books, reports and other published material, surveyed a small number of university students, and gathered 881 statements, 39 pages in all, of beliefs and attitudes held about the appearance, mental and physical traits, performance, etc., of groups classified as "socially disadvantaged" in terms of employment. This well documented and well supported study showed older workers as ranking No. 11 in order of discrimination in employment in Canada.
The following is a complete list of the 18 groups in question in the order of those most discriminated against in employment to those who are subject to lesser discrimination: (1) mental retardants; (2) hippies; (3) ex-mental patients; (4) ex-criminals; (5) North American Indians; (6) beatniks; (7) physically handicapped; (8) Negroes; (9) East European communists; (10) East Indians; (11) older workers; (12) school drop-outs; (13) Orientals; (14) southern Europeans; (15) Jews; (16) women; (17) north Europeans; (18) British immigrants. The study, however, points out that ranking would assume a somewhat different order in different geographic areas. For example, Negroes might well be ranked higher in certain areas of the United States.
In principle, I would favour such an extension and I am sure the government will in due course endeavour to determine whether it can be achieved in a practical way. In the meantime, although in sympathy with its purpose, I am unable to support this bill which would add discrimination based on age, except where based on bona fide occupational considerations, to the list of employment practices prohibited by the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. I cannot do so because I am not satisfied that the bill would meet the tests of practical application.
I think all members of the House will understand that there is a significant difference between race, colour, religion and national origin on the one hand, and age on the other. The first group of factors should never be involved in determining qualifications for employment, and for this reason it is relatively simple to deal with them by way of legal prohibitions, as the present act does.
Age is different, however. In some cases, as the bill now before us recognizes, age may be a legitimate basis for distinctions in employment. Such distinctions can derive from a desire to provide training opportunities to the
[Mr. Weatherhead.l
young or special protection to the old. They are very much a part of bona fide apprenticeship plans and pension plans, and they have a legitimate relationship to seniority provisions and other conditions of employment. For these reasons, it would clearly be unwise to force rigid and universal equality of treatment, regardless of age, by means of hasty or inadequate legislation.
Age discrimination is in many cases a question of practical distinction or economic consideration and does not always have the same form or substance as discrimination based on race, colour or national origin. Unless it provided for some flexibility through appropriate regulation-making power, age legislation could prove to be difficult or impossible to administer. Poorer employment prospects for certain age groups sometimes result from a desire on the part of an employer to maintain some balance in the age structure of his work force in order to provide for an orderly process of training, promotion and retirement, and in order to avoid the problems that can be created for both managers and employees by the lack of such a process.
Some superannuation schemes have also been a serious obstacle to the hiring of older workers. This barrier will gradually be removed through application of the Canada Pension Plan and the move toward portability of pensions. None the less, at the present time any law dealing with age discrimination should be based on careful consideration of a number of pension questions.
There is legislation in Canada and in many other countries of the world which not only permits but insists upon distinctions in work on the basis of age, particularly in connection with night work and underground work. It seems clear that since some distinctions on the basis of age are necessary, and since age is such a general and universal type of factor, a good deal of care must be taken in developing a legislative approach to the problem of discrimination in employment.
It is difficult to isolate the age factor as the full cause of any apparent discrimination in relation to employment. While chronological age is not considered a true measure of employability, no acceptable measurements of psychological and physiological age are yet available to employers to replace the date of birth method for deciding the age of a man for legitimate reasons such as pension plan rates and retirement dates. Thus questions and records which would be considered dis-
December 2, 1969

criminatory if asked or kept in connection with race or religion, would be considered non-discriminatory in relation to age.
In Canada three provinces, British Columbia, Ontario and Newfoundland, have fair employment practices legislation which prohibits discrimination based on age. In 1967 the United States government passed legislation of the same type. Several of the American states have similar legislation. In general, these laws prohibiting age discrimination permit employers to reject older workers when the rejection is based on bona fide occupational qualifications. Sixty-five is normally set as the maximum protected age.
I understand that experience under these laws is among the factors being considered by the Department of Labour in its current reexamination of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. For my part, I would hope this examination could be completed in the fairly near future, and that definite suggestions would be put forward by the government with respect to the act.
Mr. Warren Allmand (Noire-Dame-de-
Grace): Mr. Speaker, we have heard of black power, red power, youth power and woman power, and if action is not taken soon to deal with some of the problems facing our older people we will shortly be hearing about senior power. With advances in medicine, more and more people are living for longer periods. In this day and age when there is great accent on youth we are tending to ignore this factor. Not only are the problems outlined in the bill before us of concern to older people, but also of concern to them are problems in respect of pensions, income tax, medical requirements, and so forth. This bill deals with just one important aspect of the whole question.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
This matter is further complicated by the fact that because of technological change we find men dismissed from jobs at which they first started work, being retrained for other jobs in their mid-thirties, finding that work phased out again because of more technological change, and having to be retrained again. It is all very well to have a manpower retraining program for men in their forties and fifties who are put out of work because of technological change, but if we have no method of guaranteeing them work, or helping them find work once they have been retrained, we have not followed through with our remedy.

Fair Employment Practices Act
The bill put forward by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) embodies the right type of principle. He is taking the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, which has been quite successful, and suggesting we amend it to include people who are discriminated against because of age.
