Mr. Speaker, a great many members of this House welcome the opportunity that this CNR financing bill, Bill C-7 to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system and Air Canada, gives to discuss one of the important economic factors in our nation. I do not think that any other single factor plays a greater part in respect of the way we live, what we eat, the clothes we wear and the newspapers we read. I refer to transportation, which has a tremendous impact on our lives.
Those of us who over a period of years have had the benefit of a fairly good transportation system probably take for granted many of the services that are provided. However, during a trip as a member of the transport committee to the north shore of Quebec-that part of the country which people have referred to as the land of Cain; an area in which travel is very difficult-I became very concerned that the people there felt like the biblical individual who was cast out into the wilderness.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
However, we did find tremendous development going on in that area, in spite of the fact that the people had a feeling of being enclosed and separated from the rest of the world. I believe that before very long adequate transportation facilities will be provided for the area. The question of transportation seems to be on the minds of most of the people there. In fact, on the evening we flew into Labrador city one might have thought we were being mobbed and that a great meeting was being held at the airport. People
December 2, 1969
1514	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada were carrying placards which demanded to know why, in view of the $50 million in taxes that had been collected in the area, they did not have better transportation facilities. After we had been there a short while we found that the transportation facilities were far from adequate. It was interesting to see the extent to which company towns are being developed, how well laid out they are and how good are the good facilities provided by the companies, which are doing their utmost to keep the people happy and in good spirits.
However, I come back to the matter we are discussing tonight. Many of the complaints that have been made this year have been caused because both our main railways have indicated that they are going to cut passenger service. I have always felt a great deal of sympathy for the CNR and the CPR in this day and age when so much travelling is done by private motor car and only 15 per cent of the total miles travelled is left to be divided among the air lines, the rail services and the buses in our public transportation system. Not much of the pie is left to the railroads when the private individual does so much travelling in his car.
Nevertheless, there are problems which result from the continued cutting of services by the railroads. This fact was brought to my mind by an article in the Ottawa Citizen of November 12, 1969, entitled "Shades of Sir John". The article did not refer in particular to the CNR or the CPR but concentrated on the Algoma Central Railway. The article referred to the fact that when this railroad was being developed, it received certain grants, timber rights and tremendous financial assistance.
This has been the pattern in the development of our railroads in past years. My understanding is that when the railroads were being constructed in Ontario and Quebec and the branch lines about which we are speaking were being developed, railroad officials went from town to town with hat in hand. They were very gentle and kind; they did not make great demands but only indicated that if the community would sign up with them they would be of great assistance to the community.
Communities did sign up with the railroads and made special concessions in the way of property, lands, property tax concessions, assessment concessions, and in some cases outright grants to assist them in the early years of their development. Therefore, I feel


that the railroads have obligations in a great many areas of Canada because of the assistance they were given during the years of their development. As I said, this article refers to the "shades of Sir John."
When I visited the western regions of Canada with the transport committee we discussed whether the CPR rail service that has been in operation for many years, the transcontinental train called the "Dominion", should be taken off. In practically every area to which we went the briefs were very emphatic in listing the number of concessions that had been given to the railroads and the lands and property which had since become so valuable. This is the reason the railroads have an obligation to continue service in these areas, according to the briefs.
The railroads feel it is probably time to re-assess the situation. I believe there are some areas, however, wherein it is necessary for the railroads to continue service. When they finally cut off the passenger service on some of the lines, I wonder how long it will be before the entire railway service will be dispensed with and nothing will be left but railway rights-of-way throughout the country, which are of no great use for anything else because of the gravel and the embankment with which they are built. Not too much can be done with old railway rights-of-way unless the provincial governments decided to make roads out of them.
So the question of rail line abandonment raises many problems that are typical of certain areas. There was a time when the railroads had a monopoly. In those years it was thought that the trucking and bus services would never amount to anything and that people would have to use rail services or else, because there was no other way to travel. However, we found after a few years that the "or else" services became the ones that the people used. I have often felt that in those days the railroads should have become the great transportation media in our nation; they should have taken over the bus and trucking services rather than leaving it until now to do so. We know that practically all the LeX freight throughout Ontario is today being carried by trucks.
This brings me to another question. I have sometimes wondered why it would not be possible for the railways to operate small mobile units such as buses and trucks on their branch lines. In the area in which I live, for instance, both the CNR and the CPR may

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that Bill C-7 has become the vehicle whereby members can discuss the most serious matter of a national transportation policy in general and railway transportation policies in particular. I shall confine myself to speaking of railways. Coming as I do from the ci.y of Vancouver, where four railways have their termini, it will be easily understood that I have a keen interest in the question of railways. We have Canadian National Railway, Canadian Pacific Railway, the Pacific Great Eastern Railway and the Great Northern Railway. Being the termini of four great railroad systems, not only in this country but on this continent, and being a major port of Canada, we are vitally affected not only by the general national transportation policy of Canada but in particular by railway policy, not only as it affects the movement of freight and freight rates but as it affects passenger transportation.
In the main we have to deal with the CNR and the CPR. In considering those two great railroads I know that I express the opinion of hon. members from Vancouver and British Columbia in saying we take it not only for granted but as a commitment by this and previous governments of Canada, and by the CNR and the CPR, to continue a transcontinental system of railroads in respect of both
1516	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada passengers and freight, and that any diminution of that commitment constitutes a betrayal of Canada in general and of British Columbia in particular.
I would like to deal first with Canadian National Railways. A study of the CNR is most interesting and is well worth the attention of all hon. members. Without going too far back and into all the background, it is interesting to note that until the Capital Revision Act of 1952, 78 individual companies made up the Canadian National system. It was the intention of the royal commission that was appointed some four years before that to try to consolidate these 78 individual companies. As a result of the 1952 act they consolidated them into only 32 companies as at the end of last year.
The Canadian National system is still composed of 32 individual companies, and perhaps this set-up might be a partial cause of the trouble we have in operating a unified system of transportation. I believe the important fact which we should be considering at this time is one to which attention has already been drawn this afternoon by one of my colleagues-that is, that every year without exception we are faced with a bill similar to Bill C-7 which is now before us. Every year we have to pass a bill to meet the deficit of or the interest which is owed by the CNR and we have to pass a bill to guarantee payments on all its debenture issues. Mr. Speaker, I do not believe it is good enough that every year we should have to face this problem. We face it now, and unless real thought is given to the matter I would say that in perpetuity we will be facing the financial problems of the CNR and will have to advance more and more millions of dollars.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Since 1948 a royal commission has not studied Canadian National Railways. The 1948 commission obviously came up with only partial answers, as was shown in the Revision Act of 1952. I believe it is time that another and more detailed look was taken at the financial structure of Canadian National Railways. Consider, in a very brief way, the financial situation. Let us look at the year 1952, because that was the year of the Capital Revision Act. We find that the equity capital of the federal government in the Canadian National Railways was $857,573,774. That was in 1952. Just what it is at the moment, I do not know. I wanted to mention that figure,

DEBATES	December 2, 1969
and that is all I am going to say about the equity capital of the government of Canada in the CNR.
However, I want to mention in more detail what is owed by the CNR to the taxpayers through the medium of the federal government. In 1937 there was a royal commission and its purport was to try to resolve how to wipe out the CNR debt of over $1,500,000. Today, according to the balance sheet as of December 31, 1968, there is a debt maturing on January 1, 1972, of $100,000,000. Then we see advances for government railways and working capital in 1923, $16,983,762; financing and guarantee act, that is temporary loans, $218,573,683; refunding act, 1955, which was called loans for debt redemption, $451,100,000. So as of December 31, after all the royal commissions and after all the capital revision plans, the CNR still owes, outside of the capital equity, $786,657,445.
Mr. Speaker, it is my contention that to have to pass a bill every year covering more and more millions of dollars as loans, to pay interest and guaranteed debentures, is sheer stupidity. It is time we called a halt. We cannot call a halt to the administration of Canadian National Railways, but surely we can have the common sense to realize that this money will never be repaid. In the past the money was never repaid and hundreds of millions of dollars had to be wiped out. We know this money will not be repaid; it is proven by the bills we have to pass every year. Then why keep it on the balance sheet? Why have it on the books simply for bookkeeping purposes?
Why do we not face up to the issue in the way this House did last week when we recognized that we could not collect $122 million from Expo. There was no use keeping that deficit on the books and we wiped it off and forgot it. I think the time has come to do the same with the finances of the CNR. The money has been spent and we will not get it back. Get it off the books, forget it, and say to the CNR, "Boys, now you have had it. Produce, run an efficient operation, borrow the money under your own authority and capitalization, show a profit and return it to the federal government and, therefore, the taxpayers of Canada".

suggest most strongly that a second, new look be taken at this entire matter to see it we cannot put the CNR on a proper financial basis and get away from dealing with this bill year after year after year, plowing in money that we know we shall not get back.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-7 which we are now studying is entitled "An Act to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways System and Air Canada from the period from the 1st day of January, 1969, to the 30th day of June, 1970, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada."
In the Governor General's recommendation, various sums of money are specified: investment, $201 million; expenditures of $82 million for discharging certain obligations and the signature of contracts not exceeding $113 million. There is also a matter of borrowing $19 million for constructing branch lines. With respect to Air Canada, mention is made of a deal involving $165 million.


I do not wish to juggle with figures any longer than is necessary. Apart from dealing with a dry subject, one rims the risk of making miscalculations which could lead to various interpretations in connection with the matter that I want to discuss concerning the use of the money asked for by transportation companies to be handled according to their capital costs, redemption of stocks and capital revision.
The recommendation seems to cover everything, even the potential inadequacy of reserves and the use of further appropriations of parliament to eventually cover the deficit.
I have nothing against the carriers' action when they want to carry out financial transactions. It is even normal for the management of such vital services to gear their operations according to requirements.
However, I feel it is also normal for representatives of the people, who are called upon to decide whether these recommendations are justified should apprize parliament of the manner in which they want appropriations to be used by authorized carriers.
Before coming to the heart of the matter, I wish to point out that the management of major companies such as the CN and Air Canada calls for a great deal of competence and a deep sense of responsibilities to make the passenger service a profitable undertaking. Air Canada management is in a better position to do that than the CN. As a result of the increasing use of other means of transportation, passenger trains are operating steadily at a loss. The 1961-62 report of the MacPher-son Royal Commission on Transportation showed unequivocally how high were the losses sustained. It is however in order that a passenger service be maintained and it is probably one of the reasons which justify grants from the government when it sees fits.
For doubtful reasons or because of the intricacies of administrative problems in an undertaking showing a deficit, the president's salary has been set at $75,000 per annum. I point this out without malice aforethought simply to prove that officialdom takes good care of its own.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I shall indicate later that the distribution of jobs and wages of employees is dependent upon the principle of protecting the strong against the weak.
Considering it is recommended to invest in affiliated companies, this gives me the oppor-
December 2, 1969	COMMONS
tunity to tell the house that a rather big percentage of employees directly interested in investments have helped to create and increase a pension fund in order to ensure their security and that of their family when they retire.
As a result of the establishment of the Canada Pension Plan and of the Quebec Pension Plan, there were problems about portability which greatly worried Canadian Railways employees. Workers have always required, and rightly so, that the Canada Pension Plan be added to the pension plans of railway workers. Those plans, in operation for more than 35 years, have become a sine qua non condition for those who apply for jobs in a railway company. It should be noted that the pension plan is never a part of the contractual agreement between the employee and the employer. I believe the government should guarantee the rights of employees who were contributing to those pension plans when the government alone became effective.
I would like to discuss another important problem, that of railway crossings. The increasing number of accidents at railway crossings has become a matter of concern.
I know that it has been pointed out many times to government authorities, but unfortunately, they dilly-dally when decisions must be taken. The administrative machinery of bureaucracy gets into action only when an inquiry into serious accidents is called for.
For the past 50 years or so, a federal organization has a fund at its disposal, in order to build viaducts and eliminate railway crossings.
Statistics show that for the last 15 years accidents at railway crossings have caused 2,694 fatalities, 617 of them in Quebec. While accidents increase sharply, bureaucrats try to explain that they cannot do more under section 5 and section 265(2) of the Railway Act, as funds for construction or repairs were set in 1958. It is obvious that construction costs have increased since then, as the 11 per cent tax on building materials was not in force at that time.
The act should take into account priorities relating to the elimination of railway crossings. In the Saint-Eleuthere (Kamouraska) region that I represent, there are two very dangerous railway crossings.
In addition to the travelling public, two school-buses are daily exposed to serious accidents. Automatic signals have never been installed.

The government has already made, through the Transport Commission, a survey of the physical particularities of all the grade crossings in Canada. At the beginning of my speech I referred to the allocation of work and to salaries. Now I shall give some examples of what is, in my view, an irregular situation.
During the negotiations it seems impossible to agree on how to change the practice of percentage salary adjustments from which it follows that those who earn less than $5,000 or $6,000 a year get small salary increases compared to those who earn $6,000 or more. All groups of wage earners deserve increases when the collective agreements are renewed, but the distribution of the benefits should be better balanced. The steady increase in the cost of living affects the worker who earns $5,000 as much if not more than the worker who earns $8,000 or $10,000 a year. We must not forget that we have supported in the House a regulation asking the railway employees to return to work after a strike. We must admit that it is in order for us to look as closely as possible into the working conditions of those who have been compelled by law to return to work.
Before closing my remarks, I should like to point out to the House the housing and security conditions of these employees. They travel from their living quarters to then-working stations in trucks where are assembled all kinds of tools, and they are always exposed to accidents. Those who work as mechanical shovel operators are often without the services of a helper. Employees have to sleep in double deckers and suffer all the inconveniences that these involve.
We are advised that the company has launched a vast program to improve employees' living quarters. Cars now used for this purpose will be replaced by trailers, which proves that we are right in deploring the existing conditions.
But in the meantime the company continues to use these 1910 model sleeping cars for its employees. And the administration does

not see too much inconvenience in it since such accommodations have been approved by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. This shows again the preference given to the big to the detriment of the small.
I would like to have more time at my disposal to indicate a number of facts that prove the good will of some regional directors. There are, unfortunately, too many things to deal with, such as passenger service improvements, job security, automation implications, the clarification of many problems resulting from salary adjustments, special compensations-they sometimes happen- freight, and the competition between the various means of transport. Nevertheless, I would like to make what is, in my opinion, a practical suggestion.
Since CNR employees are, on the whole, very able and experienced, I venture to make a suggestion to the people in charge. Why, when changes are needed in the railway timetable, should we not seek the advice of a certain number of train conductors from various areas instead of taking only into account the reports made by the bureaucrats who more often than not prefer to use their car when the railway timetable does not suit them.
I am sure that the changes suggested by the personnel responsible for conducting the trains would be in the best interest of the passengers. This in turn would result in making the services more profitable.
In 1967, the year of Expo in Montreal, we had to abide by an irrelevant decision. During a full year, the passengers from Campbellton to Montreal had to cope with a transfer at Chambly.
I brought to the attention of the C.N.R. officials more than 25 requests for some change to be made. It took over a year of urging before they were finally granted. I am sure that those who made those decisions today acknowledge their mistake. If the employees had been consulted, I am convinced that could have been avoided.
I believe I have dealt with some vital points Which show that a full investigation should be conducted in the various administrative services of the CNR. Apart from showing that the workers' complaints are justified, it would help to clarify a situation that is confused at times, and give the whole team of workers, who have heavy responsibilities sometimes, the encouragement they are entitled to from a company such as the Canadian National Railways.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to this financing bill. Let me say a few words about what we should reasonably expect from the CNR if we are to continue to support it with public funds. One thing that concerns the people in my constituency as well as those to the east and west of it is the proposal to remove entirely or cut down on passenger train service.
I have received letters and representations from people who work on the railroad and live in areas which are served by the main line of the CNR. They are very much concerned about the service and the fact that service to their communities will be cut down. Many of these letters were written by people who make their living working for the CNR. They have informed me that there has been a lay-off of about 20 per cent in some communities as a result of poor grain sales and the slow movement of grain.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I suppose the movement of potash might be another factor. I believe there are two things which should be considered in this regard. The first is the welfare of those people who are employed by the CNR. The other of course is the welfare of those who use the facilities of the CNR. If a privately-owned and operated company in the province of Quebec or the province of Ontario proposed to lay off a similar number of employees, questions would be asked in this House. Not too long ago questions were asked in this House concerning companies which proposed to close down or restrict their operations and lay off men. I believe a publicly-owned concern should be just as responsible in respect of the men it employs as a privately-owned concern.
One person who wrote me advised there have been times very recently when the passenger train service which is to be discontinued was unable to handle the number of people who desired to use it. I have been informed
December 2, 1969	COMMONS
there have been many occasions when passengers who sought accommodation in terms of sleeping berths, and so on, were unable to obtain it.
I think we should be concerned about the type of service that is available, because if passengers are turned away or are unable to obtain the service they need, I suppose the traffic on these passenger trains will decline. I think we should also consider the type of people who use these trains. Many of them are old age pensioners, people who travel wi.h children and people who do not wish to incur the expense of air travel. Travel by train gives them a more comfortable and a more economic service. I think we might very well consider further use of both train travel and air travel as Canada expands. This would probably be more economical than the expansion of airports and increasing other air facilities.
We must also face the situation in respect of rail line abandonment on the prairies. I am not one of those who say that every branch line in the prairies should remain in service. People who live there know that there can be some modification. They plead, however, for a rational approach to this problem so that large and significant areas are not denuded of branch lines while other areas, due to competitive factors, have more lines than are needed.
When we discuss the financing of the railroad I think it is proper to take into consideration the type of service the railroad should give, because we own the railway the purpose of which is to not only make a profit but to provide the type of service needed in the area served. Within the past year I have been concerned about the abandonment of railway stations and the removal of agents from those sta ions, as well as the effect this has on the community. I have been interested in this matter especially because in some instances the people living in the areas have written to me as a Member of Parliament pointing out that they no longer have the services they need, or stating that the services have declined.

Then the CNR did not take the action necessary to look after the handling of the freight that was arriving at the village on their own trucks. But it is not logical to discontinue a service which a community needs and then say to the community, "That is your tough luck. Perhaps the next generation will not be here, anyway, and you can slug it out as you like."
These are the main things I wanted to say this evening on the bill. I hope that we will approach railway transportation in a rational fashion, in terms of a service to the total community, which is Canada, and to the many smaller communities that make up our country. If we do that, I think we can have a service that will give us what we need.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS, AIR CANADA PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my wish nor my intention to unduly delay this very important bill that is before the House of Commons, but my constituents would not forgive me if I failed
IMr. Gleave.l
DEBATES	December 2, 1969
to take this opportunity to bring to the attention of the House a problem which is pressing and urgent to those who are directly involved and who will be affected by the recent proposal made by the CNR in northern Ontario.
I wish to comment briefly on the question and the problem of run-throughs by the CNR, more properly called extended crew-runs. Some hon. members will recall that this question was a national issue in 1964 at which time it caused almost 3,COO operating employees of the CNR to book off sick, having fallen victim to some unknown malady. In other words, the company at that time was faced with a wildcat strike. This strike led to the Freedman industrial inquiry into the question of run-throughs. Today Canadian National Railways are once again proposing to run through the home terminal of Nakina, which was one of the main communities in this controversy five years ago. At the present time, the company is attempting to get agreement from the brotherhoods for this run-through.
This will be the first time that the company has in fact run through a home terminal, as opposed to a turn-around point. There is a very significant difference between those two types of communities, because in a home terminal people have put down roots and established themselves. They look to a future in which they will bring up their children; they build schools and hospital services are proud-ed. Transportation and other facilities are provided for them at great expense by the federal and provincial governments. There is the threat of ail this being wiped out by the announcement of the CNR that crews will no longer be located there; that they will have extended crew-runs. The very existence of this community is threatened.
The House should be reminded that the community of Nakina is in fact a child of the CNR; the railway created the town 45 years ago. Now they wish to desert this child and divest themselves of the responsibility for what will happen not only to the employees of the railroad but to the inhabitants of the community in which the railway has become an important industry. How is this major decision announced to the people? An ominous red and white announcement is posted at a central place in the town. We are told:
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The company has moved to begin discussions with its operating union on the effect of extending train crew-runs at Nakina-
December 2, 1969	COMMONS
On September 15 the company met in Toronto with representatives of its running trades. A major purpose of the meeting was to discuss the need for improved resthouse facilities between Hornepayne and Sioux Lookout. The company noted it could hardly decide on a new location for new resthouse facilities while the problem of extending crew-runs remained unresolved.
The company indicated that as it wished to locate the new resthouse facilities at Armstrong it would like to commence negotiations for extended runs between Hornepayne and Armstrong at Nakina with Hornepayne as home terminal.
With that little announcement, the people are told that their community will be destroyed. So they turn to their Member of Parliament and they plead that he do something to help save their town. As their Member of Parliament, I visited the community and saw almost all the people in the town, which comprises some 600 people. Every man, woman and child expressed the same opinion, that they do not want to move out of Nakina under any circumstances, regardless of the compensation they may receive for their houses.
They say, "Do something to help save our town." So one turns to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and he says, "Nothing can be done. It is a matter for the Canadian Transport Commission." The Canadian Transport Commission says, "Don't turn to us. Look to the brotherhoods; they are the ones negotiating with the company for this extended crew-run." Then the brotherhoods say, "There is nothing we can do because it is in our contract that we must negotiate with the company for material changes. You had better turn to the management of the company." The management then says, "We have to be efficient. We have to save money in order to have a better operation." The management provides a few figures and it is difficult for us to test their validity. Management claims it will save approximately $100,000 a year and about ten minutes in time. In order to save $100,000 a year and save ten minutes in time they want to destroy a town in which millions of dollars have been invested. That seems to be inefficient, a poor example of economy.
The community have looked very carefully at the problem and they have made it abundantly clear to me that they are not a reactionary group of people who want to stand in the way of technological progress. They have said so in letter after letter. They have said, "We are not against technological change. We are just against the manner in which it is being
DEBATES	1525
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada introduced. We want the CNR to make their technological changes in a way that will least affect people in the place in which they live and work."
As I have said, they looked carefully at the problem themselves and they have an alternate proposal which I will pass along to the House. But how seriously has their proposal been considered by the CNR? The company has been asked to come to the town to meet with the citizens' committee to explain very carefully what is involved and why they have taken this stand. We are unable to get these people to come and explain clearly and unequivocally how they will benefit northern Ontario by saving a few hundred thousand dollars and destroying a community.
Let us take just a moment and consider the cost to the community. With the extended run-through, $560,000 in wages will be lost; some 48 homes will be vacated; some 25 per cent of the tax revenue will be gone; the nearby Geraldton District High School will stand to lose about $28,000 a year in provincial grants when the 26 pupils from Nakina transfer out of it. In 1960 the provincial government authorized the Improvement District of Nakina to build a new three-roomed addition to the public school worth $70,000. Fully modern educational facilities for children from kindergarten to grade 8 are provided by annual provincial grants totalling $47,700. A run-through will reduce the school to two rooms leaving the remaining facilities standing empty and useless. The Nakina separate school, which now employs two teachers, will drop 40 per cent of its enrolment and only one teacher would be needed.
There are many CNR pensioners and widows living in the community, most of whom own homes. The increase in taxes will be far beyond their means. Some will be unable to sell, because who wants to invest in a community that is on the decline? Businessmen in the area will be affected by a 45 per cent drop in volume, which will result in staff reductions and the closing of small businesses. Until 1964 Nakina was a going concern. The province had invested huge sums of money with which to open up the town. Highway 584 was constructed to connect with highway 11, 42 miles away-a very expensive undertaking for the province. Ontario Hydro constructed a pole line into the town in 1958. Through federal and provincial assistance the new Geraldton District Hospital was built to serve the area. The population of Nakina, which in 1964 was 763, is now 600.

Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada
Then in 1964 the CNR made its drastic announcement of a run-through. From that point the trend has been downhill for Nakina. In 1966 the Indian Affairs offices were moved out, reducing the work force by five. In 1968, the Department of Transport weather station was moved out, taking another five employees. Now, once again, the dark shadow of the CNR looms over the community. The company has decided that new rest-house facilities at Armstrong are more important than the town of Nakina, and they claim that this run-through will save an annual sum of about $100,000.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the people of Nakina have looked at the problem very carefully and they feel that there is another possibility which can save their town and at the same time allow the railway to save the money to which it refers. They propose that a run-through at Armstrong would provide the same saving. Armstrong has a population of 400. Instead of being a home terminal, it is a turnaround point. In Armstrong only 11 employees would be affected. None of these are running crew but rather ticket, express, fuelling and bunkhouse staff. Only four of them own homes in the town. Moreover, it is highly unlikely that any of these people would have to move. As can be easily seen, a run-through of Armstrong would have a minimal effect on the town and could be effected at a fraction of the cost that would be suffered by the community of Nakina.
If the run-through of Nakina becomes an actuality, all the revenue that the province has invested in the town becomes wasted expenditure. Moreover, the province will probably be faced with even larger expenditures in the form of welfare payments for those citizens who are left without any visible means of support. The future of Nakina must also be considered. It has great iron ore potential nearby, and in a very few short years when these deposits are developed it will once again become a major community and the railway will once again seek to serve the town and will have to re-establish facilities there. We are really asking the railway management to be a little futuristic, to look at the potential of the area and not to think about saving a few dollars just at this moment.
I mentioned the alternative proposal of running through Armstrong instead of Nakina, because at Armstrong there would be minimal disruption of business. This proposal was made by the CNR in 1963. On February 5 of


that year at the call of Mr. Gonder, then vice-president of the prairie region of the CNR, a meeting was held in Winnipeg. It was attended by officers of the company as well as by representatives of three Brotherhoods. The purpose of the meeting was to give the brotherhoods notice of the company's intention to institute a series of run-throughs, commencing with the spring change of timetable. These run-throughs were to be-I mention only one-from Nakina to Sioux Lookout through Armstrong.
Repeatedly we have asked the management to come to Nakina and to explain why they cannot accept this very realistic alternate proposal made to them by the citizens' committee of the town. All we can learn is that a feasibility study has been made which shows it is better to run-through Nakina than Armstrong. We would like to see this feasibility study and examine it on our own to see whether in fact we can agree with its conclusions. We are asking that the company seriously consider this community; we ask that they have good public relations. Mr. Justice Freedman, in his report, with much wisdom made this statement:
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The nation's resources at both the federal and provincial level must be wisely used in measures to reduce to a minimum the disruptive effect on men and communities of the technological change.
I suggest to this House, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian National Railways has not acted in the best interests of the town of Nakina. I suggest that their public relations have not been such as to assure the people that their interests are being seriously considered.
Looking for a life-line, desperate to find someone to assist in preventing this run-through until possible alternative means of development or employment can be found for the town, I turned to the Minister of Municipal Affairs for the Province of Ontario. I asked if he would have his department undertake a study, which would not take very long but which would reveal how much money would be lost and how much the taxpayers of Ontario would have to bear for this so-called efficiency move, this so-called economy measure by Canadian National Railways. If the minister will co-operate in this regard, I believe that the figures will be revealing and shocking, showing that in order for the CNR to save a small amount of money, millions of dollars will have to be spent by the taxpayers of the province; an entire community will
December 2, 1S69

be disrupted, people dislocated, and the appeals of men, women and children who live there will not be taken into account to any extent whatsoever.
I bring this matter to the attention of the House because when Parliament did not take it seriously five years ago a serious national situation developed. The people of Nakina are now so desperate to save their town that I know they want to take strong measures, but I have pleaded with them not to do anything rash. I have said to them, "We must use all the channels of communication available to us in the hope that someone will listen and reconsider this move that is neither efficient nor economic.
Mr. Speaker, this has been the time for me to bring this serious matter to the attention of the House. I thank you for your patience. I do not intend to delay this bill to any extent, but I think you will sense the urgency felt by this community of people in my constituency. Like a great many small communities, they feel they have no voice. A Member of Parliament sometimes wonders what he does, living and working in this great, gothic structure; but he is more than someone who just fills up a space-he has to be a voice for those people who have no voice, and he has to represent the people who put him here.

NATIONAL DEFENCE-FUTURE STRUCTURE OF MILITIA FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 21, I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) if he could assure the House and the country that the proposed reductions in the reserve military forces of Canada would not be as severe as was first contemplated. While the minister's answer was reassuring, it nevertheless remains evident that up to that time at least strength of the reserve forces of Canada, presumably as an economy measure, there was contemplated a reduction in the I would hope and expect that the Department of National Defence and the minister would listen very carefully to men who have made a lifetime study of this problem and are conversant with it. In light of the fact that man for man reserve forces cost approximately only one-sixteenth as much as the equivalent strength of permanent military forces, I would hope that consideration to reduce the
December 2, 1969

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion reserve forces might be abandoned even at this time of strict economy.
When the regular forces are being reduced as an economy measure is the time, I believe, that the reserve forces should be maintained if not increased in strength. It is true that over the last number of years the "forces in being" concept has been very popular. I think it is recognized generally by all military experts that in this day and age of sophisticated military weapons, communications systems, and so on, it is necessary to have highly trained, professional, military people. Nevertheless, we should not go from that fact to the conclusion that reserve forces are now obsolete. There is still a very important place for the reserves.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I believe the present strength of our military reserves is at an absolute minimum. The reserve forces are capable of providing trained personnel for the reinforcement of our regular forces and serve as a channel through which young men may, if they so decide, become professional soldiers and join our permanent forces. The reserve forces may also be instrumental in providing trained subunits to support our armed forces in times of emergency. Most important, our reserve forces are most important as instruments of aid to civilian authorities and may be used in times of national disaster or to maintain law and order when police forces alone cannot do so, especially when violence breaks out in our major cities. I think it is appropriate for us to consider the necessity of carrying out domestic peacekeeping when necessary and not to consider our peacekeeping role as being confined to places like the Middle East and Cyprus.
It is very important for us to remember that the reserve forces provide a much needed opportunity for our young men to serve our country. The man who gives of his time in this way is twice as good a citizen because of it. The reserve forces provide an outlet for the loyalties and energies of those who wish to be ready to serve their country in times of national emergency. Also, the reserve forces bridge the gap, now dangerously wide, between the professional soldier and the civilian. This gap has grown wider in the last few years.
Our reserve forces symbolize our history and the unselfish service that has been given to our country. They are the symbols of the determination of our fathers and grandfathers

to preserve our way of life. I think it would be especially sad if units like the 48th Highlanders and the Toronto Scottish, those militia units of excellence, were to be phased out.
Considering the current social pressures and widespread acts of violence on this continent which were touched on by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), a vigorous program to revitalize and restore local militia units across Canada should be embarked upon. This new militia program should seek to rehabilitate and strengthen our traditional local units wihich have historic claims on public support and respect. The program should include imaginative training which would have a special appeal to young men between the ages of 18 and 30, and should be similar to that now being undertaken in Australia. Reserve training for our young men would develop discipline and the concept of service to one's country, and would altogether help to develop in our young men the ability and desire to be better citizens.
